metadata.title: Feedback Before The Commit.
metadata.subtitle: A Feedback Task Wearing Git's Clothes
metadata.purpose: Take the submit-solution skill apart in the Teardown register: the whole shape is Claude running a fixed five-step list, front-loaded with three feedback questions before any git command touches the tree. Name the trade-off — they optimized for feedback that actually gets collected, and made it structurally impossible to submit code without answering. The cost: no shortcut.

beats.narration_text: Liam here, in for Bear. You'd guess submitting a workshop solution is just a git task — commit, push, PR. It isn't. Here's what the skill actually makes Claude do first.

TIMING LAW: 20-35 word narration + lead_silence_s 0.8 to give the typing a >=9s window; verify media/B00.mp4 >= 8s and that the correction ('git' -> 'feedback') lands on screen and the full corrected question finishes typing before the clip ends.

beats.narration_text: Take submit-solution apart, and here's what you find. It's a folder Claude reads before it acts — one file inside, SKILL.md. That file lists five steps in a fixed order: ask about the workshop, show the diff, commit and push, open the PR, confirm. The order isn't decoration — Claude runs the list top to bottom, and can't skip ahead to committing.

production_viz.label: FIVE STEPS, FIXED ORDER
production_viz.caption: the interview runs before git, not after

beats.narration_text: Here's the mechanism. Step one runs before a single git command: three questions. Which subagent approach for cycle three — callable agents, spawn subagent, inline, something else? What was hardest about the workshop? One thing they'd change? Only then does Claude look at the diff. An empty diff doesn't mean finished — usually it means the wrong file was edited, so the skill has Claude ask, not assume. A full diff doesn't buy the PR either. The feedback comes first, every time.

production_viz.label: THREE QUESTIONS, THEN GIT
production_viz.caption: git waits for all three answers

beats.narration_text: Now the design choice. The PR body Claude writes carries two sections: the technical summary — subagent approach, eval score, tools dropped, skills enabled — and directly below it, the workshop feedback. Same document, both audiences. That's the whole trick — they made the git task carry the feedback form, so shipping the code and returning the notes are literally the same act. They optimized for feedback that actually gets collected. What that costs: you can't just push. Skip the three questions and the commit still lands — but the second half of that document stays blank, every time.

production_viz.label: ONE PR, TWO SECTIONS
production_viz.caption: skip the questions, and this half stays blank

beats.narration_text: Submit-solution isn't a git task with feedback tacked on. It's a feedback task wearing git's clothes — same PR, both audiences. Optimized for feedback that actually gets collected. The cost: you can't just push.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: ask it to write a short SKILL.md for a SUBMIT-SOLUTION skill — five numbered steps that put a three-question workshop-feedback interview before any git command, ending in a pull request whose body has both a code summary and the feedback. Then have it simulate running the skill on a made-up attendee. Go deeper: reorder the list so the commit happens first — what breaks about the design when you do?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to understand how a Claude skill controls the order of a technical task. A Claude 'skill' is a folder holding a SKILL.md — a numbered list of steps Claude reads and runs top to bottom. Write me a short SKILL.md for a SUBMIT-SOLUTION skill: five numbered steps that turn 'I finished my coding exercise' into an open pull request whose body has two sections — a code summary and workshop feedback. Put the feedback interview (three specific questions: which subagent approach was used, what was hardest, one thing they'd change) BEFORE any git command. Then simulate running the skill on a made-up attendee: play both roles, show me every question in order, and print the final PR body with both sections filled in.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: now reorder the steps so the commit happens first and the three questions come after. What breaks about the design when you do that — and what does 'the PR is the feedback form' actually mean once the commit has already landed?
